record.question:
A fitness application assigns North American DNS clients to a US Region and Asian DNS clients to an Asia Region. This geographic business rule takes precedence over distance or latency. Healthy fallback is allowed, and unmatched locations need a default route.

Both Regions need a multi-AZ application tier. The MySQL-compatible database requires one authoritative writer and permits regional reads with bounded staleness. A tested recovery runbook promotes a secondary Region during a primary failure and accounts for replication lag.

Which choices implement the routing and application/database design? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Route 53 geoproximity routing with distance biases as the sole mechanism for enforcing the continent-to-Region assignment.
Use Route 53 latency routing as the sole mechanism for enforcing the continent-to-Region assignment.
Use Route 53 geolocation records with a default and health-aware fallback hierarchy to direct clients to the regional ALBs.
Deploy multi-AZ application tiers and independent writable Aurora clusters in both Regions. Update the same records locally in each cluster and merge database changes nightly.

Deploy an ALB and multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling group in each Region. Use Aurora Global Database with one primary write Region and a secondary read Region, send writes through the global writer endpoint and eligible reads to regional readers, and use the tested database recovery runbook.

explanation.text:
<<3>> and <<5>> are correct. Geolocation records implement the explicit continent mapping, while a default covers unmatched or unresolved geography. Health-aware record trees permit the stated fallback. Regional application tiers and Aurora Global Database provide regional read access while retaining one authoritative primary writer.

<<1>> chooses by geographic distance and optional bias, which does not reliably enforce the required continent assignments.

<<2>> optimizes latency, a different objective from the business rule.

<<3>> needs correctly configured endpoint health checks or alias target-health evaluation throughout the routing hierarchy. Geolocation alone is not an application-readiness check.

<<4>> creates two independent writers to the same logical data and requires conflict resolution. Nightly merging does not implement the requested single authoritative writer.

<<5>> separates database promotion from DNS routing. After the database recovery operation, the global writer endpoint follows the primary. Cross-Region replication is asynchronous, so applications must enforce acceptable read staleness and account for possible data loss during an unplanned failover.

DNS geography reflects the query's inferred source location, not a verified customer address. A routing change does not promote a database, and multi-AZ capacity inside a Region does not replace multi-Region recovery.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [Route 53 geolocation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-geo.html); [Route 53 health-aware record trees](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-failover-complex-configs.html); [Aurora Global Database](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database.html).

diagram_alt: The routing rules choose a regional application, but both application Regions send writes to the same authoritative database primary.

sources.supports: Geolocation maps DNS-source geography to records, and a default record handles unmapped or unspecified locations.
Alias hierarchies need appropriate target-health evaluation and endpoint checks to select healthy branches.
One primary Region accepts writes, secondary Regions serve reads, and the global writer endpoint follows the primary after a separate database failover.

editorial_notes: Preserved answers 3 and 5 and made Select TWO explicit. Retained the repaired geographic business rule and single-writer focus, replacing the implausible DNS-synchronizes-databases distractor with independent writable databases and delayed merging.
